{{Short description|Statement in complex analysis}}
In [[mathematics]], and particularly in the field of [[complex analysis]], the '''Hadamard factorization theorem''' asserts that every [[entire function]] with finite order can be represented as a product involving its [[Zero of a function|zeroes]] and an exponential of a polynomial. It is named for [[Jacques Hadamard]].

The theorem may be viewed as an extension of the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]], which asserts that every polynomial may be factored into linear factors, one for each root. It is closely related to [[Weierstrass factorization theorem]], which does not restrict to entire functions with finite orders.

== Formal statement ==
Define the '''Hadamard canonical factors''' <math display="block">E_n(z) := (1-z) \prod_{k=1}^n e^{z^k/k}</math>Entire functions of finite [[Entire function|order]] <math>\rho</math> have [[Jacques Hadamard|Hadamard]]'s canonical representation:<ref name="conway">{{citation |last=Conway |first=J. B. |author-link=John B. Conway |title=Functions of One Complex Variable I|edition=2nd |year=1995 |location=springer.com |publisher=Springer |isbn=0-387-90328-3}}</ref><math display="block">f(z)=z^me^{Q(z)}\prod_{n=1}^\infty E_p(z/a_n)</math>where <math>a_k</math> are those [[Zero of a function|roots]] of <math>f</math> that are not zero (<math>a_k \neq 0</math>), <math>m</math> is the order of the zero of <math>f</math> at <math>z = 0</math> (the case <math>m = 0</math> being taken to mean <math>f(0) \neq 0</math>), <math>Q</math> a polynomial (whose degree we shall call <math>q</math>), and <math>p</math> is the smallest non-negative [[integer]] such that the series<math display="block">\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{1}{|a_n|^{p+1}}</math>converges. The non-negative integer <math>g=\max\{p,q\}</math> is called the genus of the entire function <math>f</math>. In this notation,<math display="block">g \leq \rho \leq g + 1</math>In other words: If the order <math>\rho</math> is not an integer, then <math>g = [ \rho ]</math> is the integer part of <math>\rho</math>. If the order is a positive integer, then there are two possibilities: <math>g = \rho-1</math> or <math>g = \rho </math>.

For example, <math>\sin</math>, <math>\cos</math> and <math>\exp</math> are entire functions of genus <math>g = \rho = 1</math>.

== Convergence exponent ==
Define the '''convergence''' '''exponent''' of the roots of <math>f</math> as the following:<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Levin |first=B. Ya |title=Lectures on entire functions |date=1996 |publisher=American Mathematical Society |others=Yurii Lyubarskii, M. Sodin, Vadim Tkachenko |isbn=978-0-8218-3316-2 |location=Providence, Rhode Island}}</ref><math display="block">\alpha := \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log N(f, r)}{\log r}</math>where <math>N(f, r)</math> is the number of roots with modulus <math>< r</math>. In other words, we have an asymptotic bound on the growth behavior of the number of roots of the function:<math display="block">\forall \epsilon > 0\quad N(f, r) \ll r^{\alpha + \epsilon}, \text{ and exists a sequence }r_k\text{ such that }  N(f, r_k) > r_k^{\alpha - \epsilon} </math>It's clear that <math>\alpha\geq 0</math>.

'''Theorem:'''<ref>{{Citation |last=Markushevich |first=Aleksei Ivanovich |title=Theory of Functions of a Complex Variable. Volume II |date=1965 |access-date= |edition= |place= |publisher=Prentice-Hall |isbn=9780139138140 |last2= |first2=}}</ref> If <math>f</math> is an entire function with infinitely many roots, then<math display="block">\alpha = \inf\left\{\beta : \sum_k |a_k|^{-\beta} < \infty\right\} = \limsup_{k\to\infty} \frac{\log k}{\log |a_k|}</math>'''Note:''' These two equalities are purely about the limit behaviors of a [[real number]] sequence <math>|a_1| \leq |a_2| \leq \cdots</math> that diverges to infinity. It does not involve complex analysis.

'''Proposition:<ref name=":0" />''' <math>\alpha(f) \leq \rho</math>, by [[Jensen's formula]].

== Applications ==
With Hadamard factorization we can prove some special cases of [[Picard theorem|Picard's little theorem]].

Theorem:<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Conway |first=John B. |author-link=John B. Conway |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-1-4612-6313-5 |title=Functions of One Complex Variable I |date=1978 |publisher=Springer New York |isbn=978-0-387-94234-6 |series=Graduate Texts in Mathematics |volume=11 |location=New York, NY |doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-6313-5}} Chapter 11, Theorems 3.6, 3.7.</ref> If <math>f</math> is entire, nonconstant, and has finite order, then it assumes either the whole [[complex plane]] or the plane minus a single point.

'''Proof:''' If <math>f</math> does not assume value <math>z_0</math>, then by Hadamard factorization, <math>f(z) - z_0 = e^{Q(z)}</math> for a nonconstant polynomial <math>Q</math>. By the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]], <math>Q</math> assumes all values, so <math>f(z) - z_0</math> assumes all nonzero values.

Theorem:<ref name=":1" /> If <math>f</math> is entire, nonconstant, and has finite, non-integer order <math>\rho</math>, then it assumes the whole complex plane infinitely many times.

'''Proof:''' For any <math>w\in \mathbb C</math>, it suffices to prove <math>f(z) - w</math> has infinitely many roots. Expand <math>f(z) - w</math> to its Hadamard representation <math>f(z) - w = e^{Q(z)} z^m \prod_k E_p(z/a_k)</math>. If the product is finite, then <math>\rho = g</math> is an integer.

== Proof ==
The proof below follows Conway's treatment of Hadamard's factorization theorem.{{sfn|Conway|1978|loc=Ch. XI, §3}}

Let <math>f</math> be an entire function of finite order <math>\rho</math>. If <math>f</math> has a zero of order <math>m</math> at the origin, write
:<math>f(z)=z^m f_0(z),</math>
where <math>f_0</math> is entire and <math>f_0(0)\ne 0</math>. Multiplying by a nonzero constant does not affect the order, so it is enough to prove the theorem under the normalization <math>f(0)=1</math>. The factor <math>z^m</math> can then be restored at the end.

Let <math>a_1,a_2,\ldots</math> be the nonzero zeros of <math>f</math>, repeated according to multiplicity and ordered so that
:<math>|a_1|\le |a_2|\le\cdots.</math>
Let <math>p=\lfloor \rho\rfloor</math>. The first step is to show that the zero sequence has exponent of convergence at most <math>\rho</math>, and in particular that
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|a_n|^{-p-1}<\infty.</math>

Indeed, let <math>n(r)</math> denote the number of zeros of <math>f</math> in <math>|z|<r</math>, counted with multiplicity. By [[Jensen's formula]], one obtains an estimate of the form
:<math>n(r)\log 2\le \log M(2r),</math>
where
:<math>M(r)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|.</math>
Since <math>f</math> has order <math>\rho</math>, for every <math>\varepsilon>0</math> and all sufficiently large <math>r</math>,
:<math>\log M(r)\le r^{\rho+\varepsilon}.</math>
Choosing <math>\varepsilon>0</math> so small that <math>\rho+\varepsilon<p+1</math>, it follows that
:<math>n(r)=O(r^{\rho+\varepsilon}).</math>
Since <math>k\le n(|a_k|)</math>, this gives
:<math>|a_k|\ge C k^{1/(\rho+\varepsilon)}</math>
for all sufficiently large <math>k</math> and some constant <math>C>0</math>. Therefore
:<math>|a_k|^{-p-1}\le C' k^{-(p+1)/(\rho+\varepsilon)},</math>
and the exponent on the right is greater than <math>1</math>. Hence
:<math>\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}|a_n|^{-p-1}<\infty.</math>

Consequently the canonical product
:<math>P(z)=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}E_p(z/a_n)</math>
converges locally uniformly and defines an entire function whose zeros are precisely the zeros <math>a_n</math>, with the same multiplicities. Thus
:<math>F(z)=\frac{f(z)}{P(z)}</math>
is a zero-free entire function. Since the complex plane is simply connected, there is an entire function <math>g</math> such that
:<math>F(z)=e^{g(z)}.</math>
Hence
:<math>f(z)=e^{g(z)}P(z).</math>

It remains to prove that <math>g</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>p</math>. For this Conway uses the following logarithmic-derivative lemma.

'''Lemma.''' If <math>f</math> is an entire function of finite order <math>\rho</math>, <math>f(0)\ne0</math>, and <math>p</math> is an integer with <math>p>\rho-1</math>, then, away from the zeros of <math>f</math>,
:<math>\frac{d^p}{dz^p}\left(\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\right)
=
-p!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(a_n-z)^{p+1}}.</math>

In the present case <math>p=\lfloor\rho\rfloor</math>, so <math>p>\rho-1</math>. Applying the lemma to <math>f</math> gives
:<math>\frac{d^p}{dz^p}\left(\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}\right)
=
-p!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(a_n-z)^{p+1}}.</math>

On the other hand, since <math>f=e^gP</math>,
:<math>\frac{f'}{f}=g'+\frac{P'}{P}.</math>
For a single elementary factor,
:<math>\frac{d}{dz}\log E_p(z/a)
=
-\frac{1}{a-z}+\sum_{j=1}^{p}\frac{z^{j-1}}{a^j}.</math>
After differentiating <math>p</math> times, the polynomial part vanishes, and hence
:<math>\frac{d^p}{dz^p}\left(\frac{P'}{P}\right)
=
-p!\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{(a_n-z)^{p+1}}.</math>
Comparing the two formulas gives
:<math>g^{(p+1)}(z)=0.</math>
Therefore <math>g</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>p</math>.

Restoring the zero at the origin, one obtains
:<math>f(z)=z^m e^{Q(z)}\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}E_p(z/a_n),</math>
where <math>Q</math> is a polynomial of degree at most <math>p=\lfloor\rho\rfloor</math>. Thus the genus of <math>f</math> is finite and is at most <math>\rho</math>. This is Hadamard's factorization theorem.
